**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 10, 2026
**Re:** Binond Releasing LLC / Favaiv Digital Cinema Services, Inc.: review of the Supply Agreement, DPA, SOW No. 1 and Mutual NDA, with recommended negotiating positions

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the four documents in the matter folder:

- Supply Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the "SA")
- Data Processing Addendum dated March 2, 2026 (the "DPA")
- Statement of Work No. 1, Theatrical DCP Mastering – US and Canada (the "SOW")
- Mutual NDA dated November 17, 2025 (the "NDA")

Three issues need to be resolved before Binond commits. In order of significance:

1. **Exclusivity is worldwide and covers every format (SA §3.1 with §§1.6 and 1.12).** As drafted, Binond must buy every distribution deliverable for every picture, in every territory, from Favaiv for at least three years. That includes streaming, home entertainment, broadcast, airline, festival and screeners. The commercial deal recorded in the SOW is theatrical DCP mastering for the US and Canada only. The SOW does not narrow §3.1, because §3.1 opens with "Notwithstanding anything in any SOW."
2. **Binond gives an uncapped, one-way data indemnity that covers Favaiv's own fault (DPA §9.1 with SA §13.3(a)).** Binond indemnifies Favaiv for all privacy claims, fines and data-subject actions "regardless of whether caused in part by Supplier." The SA cap carve-out for indemnities "under ... any Addendum" removes this indemnity from the 12-month-fees cap. A breach of Favaiv's own screener platform could therefore leave Binond with unlimited liability.
3. **Disputes would be split between New York and Delaware (SOW §9 with SA §§2.3 and 19).** The SOW chooses New York law and exclusive New York County courts. Under the SA's order of precedence the SOW prevails on matters arising under it. Day-to-day service disputes would go to New York, and Agreement-level disputes would stay in Delaware.

The NDA is consistent with the SA. It has Delaware law and a New Castle County forum, and SA §9.5 preserves it for information exchanged before the deal. I found no issue in it. A few secondary points and open items are listed in Sections 5 and 6.

**Business decisions for the client** are marked **[BUSINESS DECISION]** below. In short:
- what exclusivity scope Binond is actually willing to give;
- what cap or super-cap it can accept on the data indemnity;
- whether it will trade anything to get New York out of the SOW (unlikely to be needed).

---

## 2. Issue 1: Overbroad exclusivity (most significant)

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §3.1, read with §1.6 ("Distribution Deliverables") and §1.12 ("Territory")
- Against SOW No. 1 §1.2 (Background)
- Against SA §2.3 (order of precedence)

**What the documents say:**
- **SA §3.1:** "Notwithstanding anything in any SOW, Customer shall procure **all Distribution Deliverables exclusively from Supplier** throughout the Territory during the Term."
- **SA §1.6** defines "Distribution Deliverables" as every deliverable of any kind for any Picture Binond distributes. That covers theatrical (DCPs, KDMs, drives), home entertainment, streaming/VOD, broadcast and cable, airline and in-flight, and festival and market deliverables. It also covers all mastering, encoding, conforming, packaging, duplication, encryption and screener services relating to them.
- **SA §1.12:** "Territory" means "the entire world."
- **SOW §1.2:** "The Parties have agreed that Supplier will be Customer's exclusive provider of **theatrical DCP mastering for releases in the United States and Canada**."

**Why the SOW does not fix this:**
- SA §2.3 says that, in a conflict, "any SOW, as to the Services, Deliverables and any matters arising under that SOW" prevails over the body of the Agreement. On its own, that rule might let SOW §1.2 control.
- However, §3.1 begins "Notwithstanding anything in any SOW." That is a specific override and will very likely displace the general precedence rule.
- SOW §1.2 is also framed as a recital ("Background"). It describes the deal rather than operating as a covenant limiting §3.1.
- The SOW therefore should not be relied on to narrow the exclusivity. We should not tell the client that it does. As drafted, §3.1 controls.

**Why it matters for Binond:**
- **Lost flexibility.** For the three-year Initial Term (SA §4.1), and for any automatic one-year renewals (§4.2), Binond could not use any other vendor for:
  - streaming or VOD masters (IMF, ProRes deliverables to platforms);
  - home entertainment;
  - broadcast;
  - airline;
  - foreign-territory deliverables;
  - festival and market deliverables;
  - screeners.
- **Services not even under contract.** Many of these services have not been contracted at all. SOW §2.3 expressly excludes KDMs, drive duplication, screeners and "any non-theatrical deliverables." Binond would be locked into Favaiv for services with no agreed price, specification or turnaround, which gives Favaiv considerable leverage when any later SOW is negotiated.
- **Conflicts with pictures Binond licenses out or acquires.**
  - Licensees, sub-distributors and platforms often require their own preferred labs.
  - Acquisition agreements often come with deliverables already produced by the producer's vendor.
  - Strictly, any third-party-produced deliverable for a Binond picture would breach §3.1.
- **Weak protection if Favaiv cannot perform.** Favaiv's only matching commitment is a capacity covenant (§3.2). The force majeure step-in (§16.1) applies only after a 15-day force majeure event. Binond has no right to go elsewhere if Favaiv lacks the capability (for example, streaming QC to a particular platform's specification) or cannot meet a deadline.
- **Remedy exposure.** Breaching an exclusivity covenant risks a lost-profits claim from Favaiv. That would fall under the §13.2 cap, but it is still a dispute Binond does not need.

**Recommended fix:**
- Narrow §3.1 to the deal actually recorded in the SOW.
- Remove the "notwithstanding" language.
- Add carve-outs for third-party-controlled deliverables.
- Add a release valve if Favaiv cannot perform.

**Proposed language (replace SA §3.1):**

> **3.1 Exclusive Supply.** During the Term, Customer shall procure from Supplier, on an exclusive basis, the theatrical digital cinema package mastering services described in SOW No. 1 for Pictures that Customer releases theatrically in the United States and Canada (the "**Exclusive Services**"). Customer is free to procure any other services or deliverables, including all non-theatrical deliverables, KDM, duplication and screener services, and any services for releases outside the United States and Canada, from any third party.
>
> **3.1A Exceptions.** Section 3.1 does not apply to (a) any deliverable that a licensor, producer, sales agent, sub-distributor, exhibitor or platform requires to be produced by, or has already had produced by, a vendor other than Supplier; (b) any Picture for which Customer does not control the selection of the mastering vendor; or (c) any order that Supplier declines, cannot confirm in writing within two (2) business days, or fails to deliver in accordance with the applicable SOW.
>
> **3.1B Failure to Perform.** If Supplier fails to meet the delivery dates or specifications in an SOW on two or more Title Orders in any rolling six-month period, Customer may, on written notice, end the exclusivity in Section 3.1 for the remainder of the Term without affecting any other right or remedy.

**Conforming change:** consider deleting §1.6 ("Distribution Deliverables") altogether, or limiting it to the Exclusive Services. As drafted it serves no purpose beyond §3.1.

**[BUSINESS DECISION]**
- Confirm with the client that US/Canada theatrical DCP mastering is the full extent of the exclusivity it intended. The SOW recital suggests it is.
- Confirm whether the client wants exclusivity for future SOWs (KDMs, duplication, screeners). If so, each should be granted SOW by SOW, at agreed prices, and not swept in by §3.1.
- Confirm whether the client is content with automatic renewal (§4.2) carrying exclusivity forward. I would suggest that exclusivity apply only during the Initial Term, or that Binond be able to end exclusivity on notice at any renewal.

---

## 3. Issue 2: Uncapped one-way data indemnity covering Favaiv's own fault

**Where:**
- DPA §9.1
- Read with Supply Agreement §13.2 (cap) and §13.3(a) (cap exclusions)
- Also SA §2.3(a) (DPA prevails as to personal data)

**What the documents say:**
- **DPA §9.1:** Binond shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Favaiv against "all Losses arising out of or relating to any third-party claim, regulatory investigation, fine or penalty, or Data Subject action relating to Customer Personal Data or its Processing under the Agreement, **regardless of whether caused in part by Supplier**."
- **DPA §1.5:** "Losses" expressly includes fines, penalties, settlements and investigation costs.
- **No reciprocal indemnity.** Favaiv gives no indemnity in the DPA.
- **Supplier's SA indemnity is narrow.** Favaiv's SA indemnity (§12.1) covers only:
  - unauthorized access to *Customer Materials* (content, keys and credentials, which is not personal data); and
  - Favaiv's *gross* negligence or wilful misconduct.
- **DPA limits.** The DPA says nothing about limiting liability.
- **SA §13.2** caps each party's liability at 12 months' Fees, "except as provided in Section 13.3."
- **SA §13.3(a)** removes from the cap "indemnification obligations under Section 12 **or any Addendum**." The DPA calls itself "an Addendum made under ... the Supply Agreement" (DPA preamble; SA §1.1 expressly includes the DPA).

**Result:**
- Binond's DPA §9.1 indemnity is **not** subject to the 12-month-fees cap. It is **uncapped**.
- §13.3(a) also lifts the §13.1 exclusion of consequential damages for this indemnity.

**Why it matters for Binond:**
- **The data is sensitive and spans several regimes.** Customer Personal Data includes:
  - names, emails, credentials, IP addresses and device identifiers;
  - viewing logs and forensic watermark identifiers for critics, awards voters, buyers, exhibitors and talent;
  - festival and market attendee lists (DPA §1.2, Annex A).

  The DPA expressly anticipates CCPA/CPRA, other US state laws, GDPR, UK GDPR and PIPEDA (DPA §1.3).
- **Favaiv controls the risk; Binond pays for it.** The most likely source of a claim is a breach of Favaiv's screener platform or its sub-processors (cloud host and email provider, Annex C). Those systems are entirely within Favaiv's control. Under §9.1, Binond would still have to defend and pay Favaiv's resulting Losses, including Favaiv's own regulatory fines. That turns Favaiv's security obligations (DPA §5, Annex B) into obligations without consequence.
- **The wording reaches 100% of the loss.** "Caused in part by Supplier" is drafted to cover cases where Favaiv is substantially or almost entirely at fault. Read literally, any contribution by Binond (or arguably none, since the trigger is any claim "relating to" the data) shifts the whole loss to Binond.
- **The exposure is unlimited.** A screener leak involving awards voters or a festival attendee list could produce class claims, regulator investigations and notification costs far above twelve months of mastering fees. Twelve months of fees is likely in the tens of thousands of dollars at $4,850 per master (SOW §5.1).
- **Insurance mismatch.** Favaiv carries $3M of cyber cover (SA §14.1(c)). Binond's own policy may not respond to a contractual indemnity of a vendor's liability. This should be checked; see Section 6.
- **The DPA prevails.** Because SA §2.3(a) gives the DPA precedence on personal-data matters, Binond cannot rely on the narrower allocation in SA §12 to cut this back.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Limit Binond's indemnity to claims caused by *Binond's* breach of the DPA or Data Protection Laws (for example, failure to give notices or obtain consents under DPA §3.2, or unlawful instructions).
2. Expressly exclude claims to the extent caused by Favaiv or its Sub-processors.
3. Add a reciprocal Favaiv indemnity for its breach of the DPA, Data Protection Laws, or any Personal Data Breach in its systems.
4. Bring both indemnities under a cap: either the general cap or a negotiated super-cap.
5. Fix SA §13.3(a) so it no longer automatically removes Addendum indemnities from the cap.

**Proposed language (replace DPA §9.1):**

> **9.1 By Customer.** Customer shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Supplier and its Affiliates, officers, employees and agents from and against all Losses arising out of any third-party claim, regulatory investigation or Data Subject action to the extent caused by (a) Customer's breach of Section 3 of this DPA or (b) Customer's violation of Data Protection Laws, in each case excluding any Losses to the extent caused by Supplier, its personnel or its Sub-processors.
>
> **9.1A By Supplier.** Supplier shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates, officers, employees and agents from and against all Losses arising out of any third-party claim, regulatory investigation, fine or penalty, or Data Subject action to the extent caused by (a) Supplier's or any Sub-processor's breach of this DPA or of Data Protection Laws, or (b) any Personal Data Breach affecting systems or facilities under the control of Supplier or any Sub-processor.
>
> **9.3 Limitation.** Each Party's aggregate liability under this Section 9 is subject to a separate cap equal to [the greater of US$[●] and [●] times the Fees paid or payable in the twelve (12) months preceding the event giving rise to the claim] (the "**Data Cap**"). The Data Cap does not apply to a Party's fraud or wilful misconduct.

**Conforming change to SA §13.3(a):**

> (a) indemnification obligations under Section 12 (and, for the avoidance of doubt, indemnification obligations under any Addendum shall be subject to any limitation set out in that Addendum, or if none, to Section 13.2);

**[BUSINESS DECISION]**
- **Cap model.** The client should decide what cap or super-cap it is prepared to accept on both sides. A data super-cap of 2–3x annual fees, or a fixed dollar figure tied to Favaiv's $3M cyber cover, is a common landing point.
- **Fallback if Favaiv refuses a mutual indemnity.** The minimum position should be:
  - the "regardless of whether caused in part by Supplier" language is deleted;
  - Supplier-caused incidents are excluded; and
  - Binond's indemnity is capped.

---

## 4. Issue 3: Governing law and forum split (New York vs Delaware)

**Where:**
- SOW No. 1 §9 (§§9.1 and 9.2)
- Read with Supply Agreement §2.3 (order of precedence) and §§19.1–19.2 (Delaware law, New Castle County courts)

**What the documents say:**
- **SA §19.1 / §19.2:** Delaware law; exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New Castle County, Delaware, for any action "arising out of or relating to this Agreement." The NDA (§10) is the same.
- **SOW §9.1 / §9.2:** the SOW and "any dispute arising under or relating to this SOW" are governed by **New York law**. The parties submit to the **exclusive** jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in **New York County**.
- **SA §2.3 (order of precedence):** "any SOW, as to the Services, Deliverables and any matters arising under that SOW" prevails over the body of the Agreement. Unlike §3.1, §19 contains no "notwithstanding any SOW" language. The SOW's choice therefore wins for SOW matters. SA §2.1 says each SOW is "governed by this Agreement," but §2.3 is the specific conflict rule and points the other way.

**Result: two competing exclusive forums.**
- Disputes about mastering quality, QC, turnaround, delivery failures, acceptance and redelivery, fees and price adjustments under the SOW go to **New York, under New York law**.
- Disputes about exclusivity (§3.1), the liability cap (§13), termination of the Agreement, and the DPA indemnity stay in **Delaware, under Delaware law**.
- Many real disputes will touch both. For example, a delivery failure leads to termination of the SOW and the Agreement, and a damages claim tested against the cap.

**Why it matters for Binond:**
- **Parallel proceedings and inconsistent results.** Each forum clause is "exclusive." This invites:
  - threshold fights over which court has jurisdiction;
  - parallel proceedings;
  - higher costs;
  - possibly inconsistent outcomes, for example on whether a delivery failure was material enough to support termination.
- **Lost home forum.** Binond is a Delaware LLC and presumably chose Delaware as its home forum.
- **Different law on key points.** New York and Delaware law can differ on matters such as implied covenants, damages and how limitation clauses are construed. Different parts of one relationship would be interpreted under different law.
- **The problem will repeat.** If Favaiv uses this SOW as its template, every future SOW will carry the same split.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Delete SOW §9. Replace it with a cross-reference to SA §19.
2. Amend SA §19 so it applies notwithstanding any SOW.
3. Carve governing law and forum out of the SOW-prevails rule in SA §2.3.

**Proposed language:**

*Replace SOW §9 with:*

> **9. Governing Law and Jurisdiction.** Section 19 of the Agreement (Governing Law and Disputes) applies to this SOW and to any dispute arising under or relating to it.

*Add to SA §19 (new §19.5):*

> **19.5 Precedence.** This Section 19 applies to every SOW and Addendum, and to any dispute arising under or relating to any of them, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any SOW or Addendum or in Section 2.3. Any provision of an SOW or Addendum purporting to select a different governing law or forum is of no effect.

*Amend SA §2.3 by adding at the end:*

> ... provided that no SOW may vary Sections 3, 13 or 19 of this Agreement unless it expressly identifies the Section being varied and states that it is intended to do so.

The SA §2.3 proviso also gives general protection against Favaiv later using an SOW to vary the exclusivity, cap or forum provisions.

**[BUSINESS DECISION]:** probably not needed. This is mainly a drafting fix. If Favaiv insists on New York (for example, because its facility is there), the client should decide whether it can accept a *single* forum for everything. One forum is better than a split. My recommendation is to hold Delaware throughout, consistent with the SA and NDA.

---

## 5. Secondary points (lower priority; raise if leverage allows)

- **Narrow Supplier indemnity (SA §12.1(c)).** Favaiv indemnifies only for *gross* negligence or wilful misconduct. Consider ordinary negligence, at least for content-security incidents. §12.1(b) already covers unauthorized access to Customer Materials.
- **Auto-renewal (SA §4.2).** The Agreement renews automatically each year unless notice is given 90 days before term end. Diarise the notice date. This matters especially if exclusivity is not narrowed.
- **Sub-processors not named (DPA Annex C).** The cloud host and email provider are listed only "as notified to Customer in writing." Ask Favaiv to name them before signing, so Binond's 30-day objection right (DPA §6.1) has a baseline.
- **Supplier's state of incorporation missing.** It is left blank in the SA, DPA, SOW and NDA preambles. It should be completed, and it is relevant to service of process and enforcement.

---

## 6. Open items and information needed from the client

1. **Intended exclusivity scope.** Written confirmation of the deal terms, and whether any email or term sheet records the US/Canada theatrical-only scope. This would support the negotiating position on §3.1.
2. **Existing vendor commitments.** Any current arrangements with other labs or platforms, or any licensor or sub-distributor requirements, that §3.1 as drafted would already put in breach.
3. **Signing status.** All four documents show blank signature blocks and are dated March 2, 2026 (the NDA is dated November 17, 2025). Please confirm none has been signed. If the SA, DPA or SOW has already been signed, this becomes an amendment negotiation, and Binond may already be in breach of §3.1 if it has used other vendors since March.
4. **Fee volume.** Expected annual release slate and spend with Favaiv, so we can size the 12-month-fees cap and propose a realistic data super-cap.
5. **Insurance.** Binond's cyber and E&O policies, to confirm whether a contractual indemnity of a vendor's privacy liability would be covered.
6. **Future SOWs.** Whether drafts exist for KDM, duplication or screener services. The screener SOW in particular will trigger the DPA in practice.

I am happy to turn the proposed language into a consolidated markup of the SA, DPA and SOW once the client confirms its positions on the business points above.

**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 10, 2026
**Re:** Binond Releasing LLC / Favaiv Digital Cinema Services, Inc.: review of the Supply Agreement, DPA, SOW No. 1 and Mutual NDA, with negotiating points

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the four documents in the matter folder:

- the Supply Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the **Agreement**);
- the Data Processing Addendum of the same date (the **DPA**);
- SOW No. 1 for theatrical DCP mastering in the US and Canada (the **SOW**);
- the Mutual NDA dated November 17, 2025 (the **NDA**).

There are two significant problems, set out below in order of importance:

1. **Uncapped, one-way data indemnity (DPA § 9.1, read with Agreement § 13.3(a)).** Binond would indemnify Favaiv without limit for every privacy claim, fine or data subject action. That includes claims caused in part by Favaiv's own screener platform.
2. **Governing law and forum split (SOW § 9, read with Agreement §§ 2.3 and 19).** Disputes about the service would go to New York courts under New York law. Everything else would stay in Delaware.

I also list some secondary drafting points and items we need from the client. The NDA is consistent with the rest of the folder and raises no issues.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: Uncapped one-way indemnity for personal data claims

**Where:**
- DPA § 9.1.
- Agreement § 13.2 (liability cap) and § 13.3(a) (carve-out from the cap).
- Agreement § 2.3(a) (the DPA prevails on personal data).
- Agreement § 1.1 (definition of "Addendum").

**What the documents say:**
- **The indemnity.** Under DPA § 9.1, Binond must defend, indemnify and hold harmless Favaiv against all "Losses" arising out of or relating to any third-party claim, regulatory investigation, fine or penalty, or Data Subject action relating to Customer Personal Data or its Processing. This applies "regardless of whether caused in part by Supplier."
- **Breadth of "Losses."** DPA § 1.5 defines Losses to include fines, penalties, settlements and investigation costs.
- **One-way.** Favaiv gives no corresponding indemnity in the DPA.
- **The DPA has no cap of its own.** On its face, the DPA is silent on limits of liability.
- **The cap does not reach it.** Agreement § 13.2 caps each party's liability at the Fees paid or payable in the 12 months before the claim. Section 13.3(a) then removes from both the cap and the exclusion of consequential damages any "indemnification obligations under Section 12 *or any Addendum*." The DPA expressly calls itself an Addendum made under the Agreement (DPA preamble; Agreement § 1.1). DPA § 9.1 therefore falls outside the cap altogether.
- **No fix through precedence.** Agreement § 2.3(a) gives the DPA precedence on personal data, so the body of the Agreement cannot be used to soften it.

**Why it matters for Binond:**
- **Unlimited exposure.** Binond's liability to Favaiv for privacy claims would have no ceiling.
- **The data involved.** The DPA covers screener viewer names, emails, credentials, IP addresses, viewing logs and forensic watermark logs. It also covers festival and market attendee lists (DPA § 1.2; Annex A).
- **The regimes involved.** The DPA names the CCPA/CPRA, other US state privacy laws and, where applicable, the GDPR, the UK GDPR and PIPEDA (DPA § 1.3). These regimes carry significant statutory fines and private-action exposure.
- **The risk lands on Binond even when Favaiv is to blame.** Favaiv operates the screener platform and engages the sub-processors (DPA §§ 2.1, 6). It is the party best placed to prevent a breach. Even so, the "caused in part by Supplier" language means that if Favaiv's platform is breached through its own poor security, Binond pays Favaiv's losses, including fines levied on Favaiv as processor.
- **Binond gets nothing comparable in return.** Favaiv's indemnity in Agreement § 12.1(b) covers unauthorized access to "Customer Materials." That definition (§ 1.4) is aimed at picture and sound materials and security credentials. It does not clearly extend to screener viewer or attendee personal data.
- **Result.** Binond carries uncapped risk for data that Favaiv controls in practice, with no reciprocal protection.

**Recommended fix (drafting):**

(a) **Narrow Binond's indemnity to Binond's own fault.** Replace DPA § 9.1 with:

> **9.1 By Customer.** Customer shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Supplier and its Affiliates, officers, employees and agents from and against Losses arising from any third-party claim, regulatory investigation, fine or penalty, or Data Subject action, to the extent arising from (a) Customer's breach of Section 3 of this DPA, or (b) Supplier's Processing of Customer Personal Data in accordance with Customer's documented instructions where such instructions infringe Data Protection Laws, provided that Supplier has complied with Section 4.1. Customer shall have no obligation under this Section 9.1 to the extent any Losses arise from Supplier's or any Sub-processor's breach of this DPA, the Agreement or Data Protection Laws, or from any Personal Data Breach affecting systems under the control of Supplier or any Sub-processor.

(b) **Add a reciprocal indemnity from Favaiv.** Insert a new DPA § 9.2 and renumber the existing § 9.2:

> **9.2 By Supplier.** Supplier shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates, officers, employees and agents from and against all Losses arising from any third-party claim, regulatory investigation, fine or penalty, or Data Subject action, to the extent arising from (a) any Personal Data Breach affecting systems under the control of Supplier or any Sub-processor; (b) Supplier's or any Sub-processor's breach of this DPA; or (c) Supplier's or any Sub-processor's violation of Data Protection Laws.

(c) **Bring the indemnities under a cap or super-cap.** Amend Agreement § 13.3(a) to read "indemnification obligations under Section 12 (*other than* any indemnity under the DPA)." Then add:

> **13.4 Data Protection Cap.** Each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to the DPA, including under any indemnity in the DPA, shall not exceed [the greater of (i) [three (3)] times the Fees paid or payable in the twelve (12) months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and (ii) $[●]]. [Supplier's liability for Personal Data Breaches affecting systems under the control of Supplier or any Sub-processor shall not be subject to this cap.]

(d) **Align with Favaiv's insurance.** Favaiv already carries $3,000,000 of cyber liability cover (Agreement § 14.1(c)). That is a reasonable reference point for setting Favaiv's super-cap. We should also require Binond to be named as an additional insured.

**Business decision for the client:**
- **Cap levels.** The client needs to decide what cap or super-cap figure it can accept on its own (narrowed) indemnity.
- **Asymmetric cap.** The client should decide whether to push for Favaiv's liability for breaches on its own platform to be uncapped while Binond's stays capped.
- **Binond's own insurance.** The client should confirm whether it carries cyber or privacy cover of its own that would respond to its residual indemnity.

---

### Issue 2: New York law and forum in SOW No. 1 displaces Delaware for service disputes

**Where:**
- SOW § 9.1 (New York law) and SOW § 9.2 (exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County).
- Agreement § 2.3(b) (order of precedence).
- Agreement § 19.1 (Delaware law) and § 19.2 (exclusive jurisdiction of the courts in New Castle County, Delaware).

**What the documents say:**
- **The SOW.** It subjects "this SOW and any dispute arising under or relating to this SOW" to New York law. It also gives exclusive jurisdiction over any action arising under or relating to the SOW to the New York County courts.
- **The Agreement.** It chooses Delaware law and gives exclusive jurisdiction over any action "arising out of or relating to this Agreement" to the courts in New Castle County. Agreement § 2.1 says each SOW is incorporated into the Agreement, so on its face § 19 also covers SOW disputes.
- **The conflict is decided in the SOW's favor.** Under the order of precedence in Agreement § 2.3, an SOW prevails over the body of the Agreement "as to the Services, Deliverables and any matters arising under that SOW." Section 19 contains no "notwithstanding any SOW" language to protect it. The SOW's choice of law and forum therefore wins for SOW matters.

**Why it matters for Binond:**
- **Two forums, two bodies of law.**
  - Disputes about mastering quality, missed delivery dates, failed corrections, QC, Fees and price adjustments go to New York under New York law.
  - Disputes under the body of the Agreement and the DPA stay in Delaware. These include content security, confidentiality, the liability cap and its carve-outs, and the data indemnity.
- **Many real disputes straddle both.** A botched release-date delivery could raise SOW performance issues (New York) at the same time as cap and consequential-damages questions under Agreement § 13 (Delaware).
- **Practical consequences.** Binond faces parallel proceedings, duplicated cost, forum fights over which clause governs, and possibly inconsistent results.
- **Binond loses its home forum.** Binond is a Delaware LLC. The Agreement and the NDA both choose Delaware, which appears to be the agreed position. The SOW cuts against that for the disputes most likely to arise in practice.
- **Precedent for future SOWs.** Later SOWs (for example, for KDMs, drive duplication and screeners, which SOW § 2.3 excludes) could each pick yet another law.

**Recommended fix (drafting):**

(a) **Delete SOW § 9 and replace it with:**

> **9. Governing Law and Jurisdiction.** Section 19 of the Agreement (Governing Law and Disputes) applies to this SOW and to any dispute arising under or relating to this SOW.

(b) **Protect Agreement § 19 against any future SOW.** Add at the start of Agreement § 19:

> **19.0 Application.** This Section 19 applies to this Agreement, each SOW and each Addendum, and to any dispute arising out of or relating to any of them, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any SOW or Addendum, and notwithstanding Section 2.3.

(c) **Close the gap in the precedence clause.** Add a sentence to Agreement § 2.3:

## 3. Secondary points

These are lower priority but worth raising in the same markup.

1. **Order of precedence generally (Agreement § 2.3).**
   - **The problem.** An SOW prevails over the Agreement on "any matters arising under that SOW." That is broad enough to let a future SOW quietly override protective terms in the Agreement, such as acceptance, content security or the cap. Issue 2 is one example of this.

6. **Mutual NDA.**
